```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
```

### Introduction

This project examines the differences in educational development around the world. The quality of education among a country's population is an important indicator of the wellbeing and future advancement of a country, yet it varies significantly across different places and groups of people.

What I really love about statistics is its ability to quantitatively reveal how unequal things are across different groups of people, so that we know who might need more support.

I used data from the United Nations' Human Development Reports by the UN Development Program on the educational attributes of countries' adults 25 and older, specifically 34 years (1990 to 2023) of it from the [UNDP's open database](https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/documentation-and-downloads). Note that the variables that I'm interested in were missing data past 2023 so the past couple of years (2024 and 2025) aren't included in my analysis.

I'll focus on the following measures of educational development: the average amount of formal education attained by men and women (individually) within a country, the percentage of men and women (individually) with at least secondary education within a country, and the average amount of education attained by adults 25+ within a country. Note that secondary education, under the [UN's International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)](https://www.uis.unesco.org/en/methods-and-tools/isced), is defined as an intermediate phase of education spanning ages 11 to 18.

```{r include = FALSE}
# Loading packages
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(countrycode)
library(janitor)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

# Preparing the data
data <- read_excel("hdr-data.xlsx") %>%
  select(-c(yearStr, value, indexCode, index, dimension, note)) %>%
  filter(!(indicatorCode %in% c("gnipc", "ineq_edu", "hdi_rank"))) %>%
  mutate((across(c(year, actualValue), as.numeric)),
         continent = countrycode(countryIsoCode,
                                 origin = "iso3c",
                                 destination = "continent"),
         # NRO is for Naoero, a country in Oceania
         # ZZK.WORLD means the global value
         continent = ifelse(countryIsoCode == "NRO", "Oceania", continent),
         # Cleaning up a country name
         country = ifelse(country == "Congo (Democratic Republic of the)",
                          "Democratic Republic of the Congo", country))

# Checking for missing values
colSums(is.na(data))
# 218 NAs in "continent", but these are just world values instead
unique(data[is.na(data$continent), ]$countryIsoCode) # ZZK.WORLD

# Checking for duplicate rows
anyDuplicated(data) # 0

# Checking for duplicate (year, country, continent, indicator) combinations because there should
# only be one indicator per country per year
get_dupes(data, year, country, continent, indicator) # no duplicate combinations found
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Getting the MYS in 1990 and 2023
mys_1990 <- pull(filter(data, indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 1990), actualValue)
mys_2023 <- pull(filter(data, indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 2023), actualValue)
```

### Gender inequality

To view educational inequalities in terms of gender, I'm using two metrics: (1) the average amount of formal education attained by each gender, and (2) the percentage of adults in each gender who have at least some level of secondary education.

Here are graphs of these metrics by gender worldwide:

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by gender over time
p1 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, colour = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("mys_m" = "#4a72b8", "mys_f" = "#f8766d"),
                    labels = c("mys_m" = "Males", "mys_f" = "Females")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years"),
                     limits = c(0, 10)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "", colour = "",
       title = "Mean Amount of Education of Adults*") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = c(0.15, 0.9))

# Graphing the percentage of people who have secondary education by gender over time
p2 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, fill = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("se_m" = "#4a72b8", "se_f" = "#f8766d"),
                    labels = c("se_m" = "Males", "se_f" = "Females")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "", fill = "",
       title = "Percent of Adults* With Secondary Education") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = c(0.15, 0.9)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE))

(p1 | p2) + plot_annotation(title = "Gender Inequality in Education Worldwide (1990-2023)",
                            theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5)),
                            caption = "*Adults 25+")
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Creating a wider data frame with indicators as separate columns
wider_data <- data %>%
  group_by(year, country, continent, countryIsoCode, indicatorCode) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue) %>%
  # Getting the yearly gender gaps
  mutate(gap_mys = mys_m - mys_f,
         gap_se = se_m - se_f)
```

For both metrics, the amount for females has never been more than for males: although they've been increasing at similar speeds --- the lines in both charts are nearly parallel --- there has always been a gap of around one year or `r round(mean(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent))$gap_se), 0)` percentage points. However, the gap has been shrinking for the past few years. In 2020, the magnitude of the gap dropped to a new low of `r round(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent), year == 2020)$gap_mys, 1)` years, to `r round(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent), year == 2021)$gap_mys, 1)` years in 2021 and 2022, and `r round(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent), year == 2023)$gap_mys, 1)` years in 2023. Similarly, the percentage of males vs. females with secondary education worldwide shrunk to `r round(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent), year == 2023)$gap_se, 0)` percentage points in 2023.

So where specifically in the world do the highest gender gaps consistently occur?

To answer this question, I found the countries that ranked in the highest 10 countries at least once during the 34-year period, in terms of the gender gap for both metrics simultaneously. Then, I calculated the average gender gaps for each metric as a simple subtraction such that a positive gender difference mean that males had higher values. Note that the tie-breaking method included all countries of the same rank if there was a tie.

```{r echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Getting the countries with the largest gender gaps
high_gender_gap <- wider_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(rank_mys = rank(desc(gap_mys), ties.method = "min"),
         rank_se = rank(desc(gap_se), ties.method = "min")) %>%
  filter(rank_mys <= 10 & rank_se <= 10) %>%
  ungroup()

# Creating a table of the countries with consistently high gender gaps
high_gender_gap %>%
  group_by(continent, country) %>%
  summarize(times_in_top_10 = n(),
            mean_gap_mys = mean(gap_mys, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_gap_se = mean(gap_se, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  select(-c(mean_gap_mys, mean_gap_se)) %>%
  arrange(desc(times_in_top_10)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             country = "Country",
             times_in_top_10 = "# of Times in Highest 10") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With Consistently High Gender Gaps* (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#F0F0F0"),
            locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything())) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE) %>%
  tab_source_note(source_note = "*Ranked in terms of both the average amount of education and the percentage with secondary education (in each gender for adults 25+) simultaneously.")
```

There are 15 countries in this table (out of `r n_distinct(data$countryIsoCode)` total countries in the data), of which the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Liberia have been there in 34 of the 34 years.

Here's a similar breakdown by continent:

```{r echo=FALSE}
high_gender_gap %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            pct = round(n/nrow(high_gender_gap) * 100, 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(pct)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             n = "# of Times in Highest 10",
             pct = "% of Countries") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Continents With Consistently High Gender Gaps* (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#F0F0F0"),
            locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything())) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE) %>%
  tab_source_note(source_note = "*Ranked in terms of both the average amount of education and the percentage with secondary education (in each gender for adults 25+) simultaneously.")
```

The only continents in this table are Africa and Asia. The rightmost column shows the percent share of countries that belong to that continent.

To visualize the most recent year of data for these countries, I plotted graphs showing their states in 2023, ordered by descending gender gap according to their metric. My main observation is that the gender gaps were quite similar among the selected countries; they ranged from 2 to 4 years and 20 to 25 percentage points wide.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
high_gender_gap <- high_gender_gap %>%
  group_by(continent, country) %>%
  summarize(times_in_top_10 = n(),
            mean_gap_mys = mean(gap_mys, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_gap_se = mean(gap_se, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

ordered_countries_mys <- pull(arrange(high_gender_gap, mean_gap_mys), country)
ordered_countries_se <- pull(arrange(high_gender_gap, mean_gap_se), country)

p3 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"),
         country %in% high_gender_gap$country,
         year == 2023) %>%
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = ordered_countries_mys)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = country, y = actualValue, fill = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("mys_m" = "#4A72B8", "mys_f" = "#F8766D"),
                    breaks = c("mys_m", "mys_f"),
                    labels = c("mys_m" = "Males", "mys_f" = "Females")) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 13),
                     labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Mean Education", fill = "") +
  theme_minimal()

p4 <- high_gender_gap %>%
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = ordered_countries_mys)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = country, y = mean_gap_mys)) +
  geom_col(fill = "gray30") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 13),
                     labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Gender Gap") +
  theme_minimal()

p5 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"),
         country %in% high_gender_gap$country,
         year == 2023) %>%
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = ordered_countries_se)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = country, y = actualValue, fill = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("se_m" = "#4A72B8", "se_f" = "#F8766D"),
                    breaks = c("se_m", "se_f"),
                    labels = c("se_m" = "Males", "se_f" = "Females")) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Percent With Secondary Education", fill = "") +
  theme_minimal()

p6 <- high_gender_gap %>%
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = ordered_countries_se)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = country, y = mean_gap_se)) +
  geom_col(fill = "gray30") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Gender Gap") +
  theme_minimal()

(p3 | p4) / (p5 | p6) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Magnitude of Gender Gaps in Education in 2023",
                  subtitle = "The countries included are the ones with a gender gap in the highest 10 in term of both metrics at least once from 1990 to 2023.",
                  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5)))
```

### Geographic inequality

Next, I view the geographic variation in terms of the average amount of education for adults to contrast individual continents and countries.

I created a graph of each continent's average amount of education:

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by continent over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarise(mean_mys = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(continent = factor(continent,
                            levels = c("Europe", "Oceania", "Americas", "Asia", "Africa"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_mys, colour = continent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "", y = "",
       title = "Mean Amount of Education of Adults* by Continent (1990-2023)",
       colour = "Continent",
       caption = "*Adults 25+") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2")
```

From this graph, we see that the absolute rankings have been the same since 1990 and that every continent except for Oceania has grown at a similar rate. In 2023, Oceania, the Americas, and Asia were all at similar places (all around an 8-year average) while Europe and Africa remained higher and lower (respectively) than these three continents, both by 4 years. But this graph is still encouraging --- despite the fact that the absolute rankings haven't changed, all continents have steadily grown through the past few decades at least.

```{r include=FALSE}
# Getting the yearly gaps
widest_gaps <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", !is.na(continent), !is.na(actualValue)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(lowest = country[which.min(actualValue)],
            highest = country[which.max(actualValue)],
            gap = round(max(actualValue) - min(actualValue), 1),
            .groups = "drop")
```

To further get a sense of the widest differences globally, here are the highest and lowest-ranked countries from 1990 to 2023:

```{r echo=FALSE}
widest_gaps %>%
  # Creating variables for each distinct year group per country group
  mutate(new_group = lowest != lag(lowest, default = first(lowest)) |
                highest != lag(highest, default = first(highest)),
         group_id = cumsum(new_group)) %>%
  group_by(group_id, lowest, highest) %>%
  summarise(min_year = min(year),
            max_year = max(year),
            year_range = paste(min_year, max_year, sep = " - "),
            mean_gap = mean(gap, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  select(year_range, lowest, highest, mean_gap) %>%
  mutate(year_range = replace_when(year_range,
                                   year_range == "2003 - 2003" ~ "2003",
                                   year_range == "2004 - 2004" ~ "2004")) %>%
  arrange(year_range) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(year_range = "Year Range",
             lowest = "Lowest Country",
             highest = "Highest Country",
             mean_gap = "Average Gap (Years)") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Biggest Gaps in Education by Country (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#F0F0F0"),
            locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything())) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE)
```

The differences range from `r round(min(widest_gaps$gap), 1)`-`r round(max(widest_gaps$gap), 1)` years and have a small standard deviation of `r round(sd(widest_gaps$gap), 1)` years, again because the rate of growth has been similar worldwide. Niger and Germany appear with the highest frequency, each appearing 4 times. The US appears twice, and Yemen, Mali, Burkina Faso, and New Zealand appear once, which indeed reflects the state of the continental rankings.

Once again, I want to know which countries have the most consistently low averages from the full range of the data, so here are the countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once (in terms of the average amount of education of its population over 25 years):

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Getting the least educated countries in terms of the mean (1990-2023)
bottom_countries <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(actualValue, ties.method = "min")) %>%
  filter(rank <= 10) %>%
  ungroup()

# Making a table of the countries with consistently low education rates
bottom_countries %>%
  count(continent, country, name = "times_in_bottom_10") %>%
  arrange(desc(times_in_bottom_10)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             country = "Country",
             times_in_bottom_10 = "# of Times in Bottom 10") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With Consistently Low Education Rates (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#F0F0F0"),
            locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything())) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE)
```

There are 17 countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once, of which 4 countries (Afghanistan, Guinea, Mali, and Niger) have been there in every year of the 34.

Here's a similar breakdown by continent:

```{r echo=FALSE}
bottom_countries %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            pct = round(n/340 * 100, 2)) %>%  # 340 because 34 years * bottom 10
  arrange(desc(pct)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             n = "# of Times in Bottom 10",
             pct = "% of Countries") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Continents With Consistently Low Education Rates (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#F0F0F0"),
            locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything())) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE)
```

Now to focus on 2023 again, I found the countries in the lowest 10 in 2023:

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
bottom_countries_2023 <- data %>%
  filter(year == 2023, indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  arrange(actualValue) %>%
  mutate(difference_from_world = mys_2023 - actualValue) %>%
  select(continent, country, actualValue, difference_from_world) %>%

bottom_countries_2023 %>%

```

And the highest 10:

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
top_countries_2023 <- data %>%
```

I distilled this information into a graph:

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
bottom_countries_2023 %>%
  rbind(top_countries_2023) %>%
  mutate(continent = factor(continent, levels = c("Europe", "Americas", "Asia", "Africa"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, -difference_from_world), y = -difference_from_world, fill = continent)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Most Extreme Countries in Terms of Average Education in 2023",
       x = "", y = "Difference From World Average (Years)",
       fill = "Continent") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Europe" = "#66C2A5",
                               "Americas" = "#8DA0CB",
                               "Asia" = "#E78AC3",
                               "Africa" = "#A6D854")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-7.5, 7.5)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 10.5), linewidth = 0.75, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 10.5, xmax = 20.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf), alpha = 0.015, fill = "grey70") +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0, xmax = 10.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf), alpha = 0.015, fill = "grey30") +
  theme_minimal()

# Getting the MYS in 1990 and 2023 for Africa

mys_africa_1990 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", continent == "Africa", year == 1990) %>%
  with(mean(actualValue))

mys_africa_2023 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", continent == "Africa", year == 2023) %>%
  with(mean(actualValue))
```

Africa appears 9 times and Asia appears once in the bottom 10. Europe appears 7 times, Americas appears twice, and Asia appears once in the top 10. (The rest of the countries are obviously just between these two extremes.) Clearly, the asymmetry between the two extremes was still quite striking in 2023 despite Africa's steady growth through the years which nearly doubled its mean education amount from `r round(mys_africa_1990, 1)` years in 1990 to `r round(mys_africa_2023, 1)` years in 2023.

### Summary

The main findings of my analysis are:

1. Both gender and geographic educational inequality on the world level have remained consistent from 1990 to 2023, if only because they’ve been unequal since 1990 and have improved at similar speeds across continents.
2. For gender inequality, the most consistently unequal areas have occurred in Africa and Asia, which have respectively made up 70% and 30% of the countries that have ever made the most unequal 10 from 1990 to 2023. Specifically, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Liberia have been among the most unequal countries in all 34 years.
3. For geographic inequality, Africa and Asia have the largest share of the most consistently lowest-average areas, which have respectively made up 84% and 16% of the countries that have ever made the lowest 10 from 1990 to 2023. Specifically, Afghanistan, Guinea, Mali, and Niger have been among the lowest countries in all 34 years.
4. In 2023, the largest gender gaps at the country level were 4 years and 25 percentage points wide, and the largest geographic gap occurred between Niger and Germany and was 12.9 years wide.

Lastly, I want to mention that this study isn't perfect. For example, regarding the data, there was likely undersampling, which compromises how representative my results are. In addition, education is only one take on a country's level of development, and I could delve deeper into why these educational disparities exist and whether there are meaningful relationships between gender, geographic, and other types of inequality. But again, what I love about statistics is its ability to quantitatively demonstrate real inequalities --- in order to help real people --- and hopefully this study shows one way to do that.
